title: The Print Function

items.title: The Anatomy of print()
items.content:
In Python, `print()` is a **built-in function**.

A function is like a tool that does a specific job. When you call a function, you write its name followed by parentheses `()`.

The values you place inside the parentheses are called **arguments** (or inputs). The `print()` function takes whatever arguments you give it and displays them on your screen.
items.explanation: In Python, `print()` is a **built-in function**. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: In the statement `print("Welcome!")`, what is the term for `"Welcome!"`?
options: B. The argument (input) passed to the function
items.explanation: Values passed into a function inside its parentheses are known as arguments.

items.title: Printing Multiple Items
items.content:
You can print multiple items in a single `print()` call by separating them with a **comma** `,`:
```python
print("Level:", 5)
```
Output:
`Level: 5`

Notice that Python automatically puts a single space between each item separated by a comma!

items.title: The Default Newline
items.content:
By default, every `print()` statement ends with an invisible newline character (`\n`). That is why consecutive `print()` statements appear on separate lines:
```python
print("Line 1")
print("Line 2")
```
Output:
```text
Line 1
Line 2
```
items.explanation: By default, every `print()` statement ends with an invisible newline character (`\n`). Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.title: Controlling the Line End with end=
items.content:
You can change how `print()` finishes its line using the `end` keyword argument:
```python
print("Hello", end=" ")
print("World")
```
Output:
`Hello World`

Instead of jumping to a new line, Python ended the first print with a space, so the next print started on the exact same line.

items.title: Custom Separators with sep=
items.content:
When printing multiple arguments, Python puts a space between them by default (`sep=" "`).

You can customize this separator using `sep=`:
```python
print("2026", "10", "03", sep="-")
```
Output:
`2026-10-03`
items.explanation: When printing multiple arguments, Python puts a space between them by default (`sep=" "`). Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.title: Escape Characters: \n and \t
items.content:
A backslash `\` inside a string creates an **escape sequence** that represents special characters:

* `\n`: Inserts a new line
* `\t`: Inserts a tab (indentation space)
* `\\`: Inserts a literal backslash
* `\"`: Inserts a literal double quote inside double quotes

Example:
```python
print("Hello\nWorld")
```
Outputs 'Hello' on one line and 'World' on the next.
